blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Calculate PES from data with the formula, read the value that results, and interpret what a supply diagram shows about sellers' responsiveness, including the vertical, horizontal and unit-elastic supply curves.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: The formula and its reading
blocks.text: PES = percentage change in quantity supplied / percentage change in price. Each percentage is worked on the original figure: the change divided by the starting level, times 100. A value above 1 shows elastic supply - the quantity offered changed by a larger percentage than the price did - and a value below 1 shows inelastic supply, where the quantity offered changed by a smaller percentage.

blocks.heading: Kaoko Juice works one out
blocks.text: Kaoko Juice bottles marula juice at Opuwo. When the wholesale price of a crate rose from N$100 to N$110, the crates it offered each week rose from 200 to 260. Step one, the percentage change in quantity supplied: crates rose by 60, since 260 - 200 = 60 crates, so the change is 60 / 200 = 30%. Step two, the percentage change in price: the price rose by N$10, since 110 - 100 = N$10, so the change is 10 / 100 = 10%. Step three, the ratio: PES = 30 / 10 = 3. The bottler's supply is elastic, and the figure carries no units.

blocks.heading: Reading a supply curve's steepness
blocks.text: A supply diagram shows elasticity without numbers. Price sits on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, and the steepness of the supply curve carries the reading. A steep curve shows inelastic supply - a large price change moves the quantity offered little, as with fresh fish already landed at Walvis Bay. A flatter curve shows elastic supply - a small price change moves the quantity offered a lot, as with T-shirts a Katutura workshop prints within hours. When demand shifts, the shift tends to land mostly on price where supply is inelastic and mostly on quantity where it is elastic: coffee already picked in Brazil cannot answer this season's price.

blocks.heading: Three special values: 0, 1 and infinity
blocks.text:
As with demand, three values of PES have names of their own and curve shapes to match.

Perfectly inelastic supply, PES = 0. The quantity offered does not change at all when the price changes, so the supply curve is a vertical line at that quantity. The seats in a stadium on cup-final day, the fish already landed at Walvis Bay that morning and the plots in a fully built city centre are close to this case: however high the price climbs, no more can be offered in the period. A rise in demand then lands wholly on the price.

Perfectly elastic supply, PES = infinity. Sellers will offer any quantity buyers want at one price, but none at all at a lower price. The supply curve is a horizontal line at that price. A printing workshop in Katutura that can print any number of T-shirts at the same cost each, and will sell them at N$80 but not for less, is close to this case over the range of orders it receives. A rise in demand then lands wholly on the quantity sold, and the price does not move.

Unit elasticity, PES = 1. The quantity supplied changes by the same percentage as the price. Any straight-line supply curve drawn through the origin has a PES of 1 all along it, whatever its slope: if 1 000 eggs a week are offered at N$2 and 1 250 at N$2.50, both quantity and price rise by 25 per cent. A useful rule for straight lines follows from this: a supply curve that starts from the price axis is elastic, one that starts from the quantity axis is inelastic, and one that starts from the origin has unit elasticity.

Real supply curves lie between the vertical and the horizontal extremes, and the determinants in the next section explain where.
